title: The Four-Day Working Week
description: A radio report, a debate, an interview with a manager and a reflective talk about working four days instead of five.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio report
parts.intro: You will hear a radio reporter, Anna, presenting the results of a trial of the four-day working week.

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: Last year, thirty companies took part in a six-month trial of the four-day working week. Employees were paid the same salary for working four days instead of five, on one condition: output had to be maintained. The results, published this week, have reignited a debate that has been running for decades.

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: Most firms reported that productivity held steady, and a few even recorded higher revenue. Staff reported lower stress, and fewer people resigned during the trial than in the same period the year before. Perhaps unsurprisingly, almost every employee said they wished to continue.

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: But the details deserve attention. The companies that volunteered were mainly small, office-based businesses, such as design studios and software firms, where the work can be planned flexibly. Only two were in manufacturing, and none were hospitals or schools, where the hours are dictated by the people who need the service.

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: The researchers themselves are cautious. They point out that companies that volunteer for a trial are, almost by definition, the ones that expect it to work. They also note that the biggest gains came from cutting meetings and unnecessary reporting rather than from people simply working faster.

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: That last finding interests me most. If a firm can remove so much waste in a four-day week, one might ask why it was there in a five-day week. Is the shorter week the cause of the improvement, or merely the excuse to make changes that were always possible?

script.speaker: Anna
script.text: In the next part of the programme, two guests give their view.

parts.title: Part 2 · A debate
parts.intro: You will hear an economist, Dr Kerr, and a business owner, Mr Doyle, debating the four-day week.

script.speaker: Dr Kerr
script.text: The evidence is now hard to ignore. Output held, absence fell, resignations fell. If a medicine produced results like that, we'd be rolling it out. Employers who resist are defending a habit, not a principle.

script.speaker: Mr Doyle
script.text: With respect, that's a very comfortable argument for an academic. I run a small catering company. If my kitchen is closed on a day, my customers go elsewhere, and they don't come back. I can't compress five days of work into four, because the work is the cooking.

script.speaker: Dr Kerr
script.text: I accept that some sectors are different, and nobody is proposing the same rule for everyone. But even in your case, couldn't you stagger the staff, so that each person works four days while the kitchen stays open?

script.speaker: Mr Doyle
script.text: Then I need to hire more people to cover the gaps, which means higher costs and probably higher prices. It's easy to say employees should have the same pay for less time when the bill isn't yours.

script.speaker: Dr Kerr
script.text: Higher costs are a fair concern, but you should set them against what you currently lose. Staff turnover is expensive. Recruiting and training a replacement can cost a large fraction of a year's salary. If a shorter week keeps people, the saving may cover the extra cost, or at least a good part of it.

script.speaker: Mr Doyle
script.text: May. Not will. And I notice that you keep returning to well-paid office workers. What about the cleaner or the delivery driver, whose income depends on hours worked? For them, four days might simply mean a smaller pay packet.

script.speaker: Dr Kerr
script.text: That's the strongest objection you've raised, and I won't pretend there's an easy answer. It does mean the policy needs designing with care, so that it doesn't widen the gap between secure jobs and insecure ones.

script.speaker: Mr Doyle
script.text: Well, on that we can agree. I'm not against change. I'm against being told that one solution suits everyone.

parts.title: Part 3 · An interview with a manager
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Minh, interviewing a manager called Sarah about her company.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Sarah Cole manages a software company of forty people that moved to a four-day week eighteen months ago. Sarah, was it a hard sell to your directors?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: Very. One director said it would be the beginning of the end. What persuaded them in the end was that we agreed on a trial with clear targets, and that we could return to five days with a month's notice if the numbers slipped.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: And did they slip?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: For the first six weeks, honestly, yes. Customer response times got longer, and a couple of people found they simply moved their work to the evenings, which defeats the whole point. We had to change how we worked rather than just shorten the week.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Such as?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: We banned meetings on Mondays... no, sorry, on Wednesdays, which is our long block of focus time. We limited meetings to thirty minutes, and we stopped copying everyone into every message. Honestly, some of those changes were overdue, and we should have made them years ago.

script.speaker: Minh
script.text: Has anyone left?

script.speaker: Sarah
script.text: Only one person, who retired. And when we advertised last spring, we had four times as many applications as before. Candidates told us they'd read about the shorter week. For a small firm competing with big employers, that's a real advantage.

parts.title: Part 4 · A radio talk
parts.intro: You will hear a sociologist, Dr Fraser, giving a radio talk about the history of the idea of shorter working hours.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: The idea that we should work fewer hours is not new. In the nineteen thirties, a famous economist predicted that by now we would work fifteen hours a week, because technology would have made us so productive. He was right about the productivity and entirely wrong about the leisure.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: What went wrong? Partly, our appetite for goods grew as quickly as our output. But partly, I'd argue, work acquired a moral meaning. We came to treat being busy as proof of being valuable, so that a person who finishes early is suspected of laziness rather than praised for efficiency.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: This helps explain why the four-day week provokes such strong feelings. The debate is rarely only about hours and wages. It is about what a person is worth, and what a society thinks time is for.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: Supporters say the shorter week gives people time for family, study and rest, which in turn makes them better workers. That is probably true, but I find the argument slightly uncomfortable, because it still justifies leisure by its usefulness to employers. Rest, surely, needs no such justification.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: Critics, for their part, worry about fairness between those who can shorten their hours and those who cannot. That worry is legitimate, and no trial of thirty offices can settle it. Only a much wider experiment, including shops, hospitals and factories, could.

script.speaker: Dr Fraser
script.text: My own view is that the four-day week will spread unevenly, sector by sector, rather than arrive by decree. And the real test will not be whether productivity survives, but whether people feel, a few years on, that their lives have genuinely changed.

questions.text: What condition did the companies have to meet during the trial?
options: They had to work five days in busy months.
They had to hire more staff.
They had to reduce employees' pay.
They had to keep output at the same level.
questions.explanation: Staff kept their salary on one condition: output had to be maintained.

evidence.quote: output had to be maintained

questions.text: Why are the researchers cautious about the results?
options: Only a few firms reported higher revenue overall.
Many employees said they did not want to continue.
The trial lasted far too long to be reliable.
The firms taking part expected it to succeed.
questions.explanation: Volunteers are almost by definition firms that expect it to work, so the sample may be biased.

evidence.quote: the ones that expect it to work

questions.text: According to the researchers, where did the biggest improvements come from?
options: longer lunch breaks and shorter working days
cutting meetings and unnecessary reporting
employees simply working a lot faster than before
hiring specialist managers to plan the work
questions.explanation: The biggest gains came from cutting meetings and unnecessary reporting.

evidence.quote: cutting meetings and unnecessary reporting

questions.text: Why does Anna mention hospitals and schools?
options: to say that they refused to take part in the trial
to show some kinds of organisation were missing
to suggest they have too many meetings and reports
to explain why manufacturing firms did so well

questions.text: What doubt does Anna raise at the end?
options: whether staff were really less stressed afterwards
whether companies will change their working policy
whether the results were published too early
whether the shorter week caused the improvement
questions.explanation: She asks if the shorter week is the cause or merely an excuse to make changes that were always possible.

evidence.quote: merely the excuse to make changes that were always possible

questions.text: How does Dr Kerr view employers who resist the four-day week?
options: They are right to wait for more evidence first.

questions.text: What is Dr Kerr suggesting when she mentions staff turnover?
options: Replacing staff is cheaper than introducing a shorter week.
Doyle should hire more people to cover gaps right now.

The saving from keeping staff could offset the cost.

questions.text: How does Dr Kerr respond to Mr Doyle's point about low-paid workers?
options: She offers a simple solution.
She dismisses it as unrealistic.
She says it does not apply to cleaners.
She admits it is a serious difficulty.
questions.explanation: She calls it the strongest objection and says there is no easy answer.

evidence.quote: That's the strongest objection you've raised

questions.text: What do the two speakers agree on at the end?
options: The policy should be introduced at once.
Businesses should pay for the change.
A single approach will not suit every worker.
Office workers should work fewer days than others.
questions.explanation: Kerr says the policy needs careful design, and Doyle agrees, objecting to one solution for everyone.

evidence.quote: the policy needs designing with care

whether people feel their lives have improved
whether employers continue to support it
whether productivity survives the change
